messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Vignette:
Mateo is a 22-year-old single Latino man working as a product manager at a fast-growing tech company, and when he began treatment he spoke about his symptoms in a matter-of-fact way that made clear how ordinary they had come to feel to him. The event he returned to was a period spent as a civilian in a war zone, where daily life had narrowed into watching, listening, and reacting quickly enough to stay alive. He described moving through streets where danger could arrive without warning, learning to read the smallest changes around him, and bracing at sudden movement because in that setting movement nearby could mean immediate threat. What stayed with him was not only fear during those days, but the sense that his body had learned something permanent there: that safety could vanish in an instant, and that failing to notice one sign soon enough could cost him everything.

In the weeks after he left the war zone, Mateo expected the tension to fade once he was back in the United States. Instead, he noticed that his body remained tight and prepared, as if some part of him still assumed that danger was close. He sat with his shoulders raised, jaw clenched, and legs ready to move. He began paying close attention to his body, checking repeatedly for signs that something was wrong. A brief pain in his chest, a twitch in his arm, a rush of adrenaline after hearing someone pass behind him would send him inward immediately, scanning himself for injury or for evidence that he was about to lose control. He found it difficult to trust his own body. If his heart was pounding, he wanted to know why. If he felt shaky, he looked for what it meant. He kept trying to determine whether he was actually safe.

That vigilance followed him into his workday. As a product manager, Mateo spent much of his time in open-plan meetings, moving between conference rooms, desk clusters, and crowded hallways. Those spaces became especially difficult because he was intensely reactive to unexpected movement nearby. A coworker standing up suddenly beside him, someone passing close behind his chair, or a hand entering his peripheral vision during a meeting could make him jerk, tense, or turn sharply as if he were defending himself. He was embarrassed by how quickly his body reacted, but in the moment it never felt exaggerated; it felt necessary. He had become superalert, constantly watching entrances, tracking where people were standing, and noticing shifts in the room before he could focus on the conversation itself. By the end of the day he was exhausted from staying on guard.

Outside work, Mateo increasingly leaned on other people to help him decide whether he was okay. He texted friends, called family members, and asked versions of the same question again and again: Did he seem normal? Did they think he was safe? Was it bad that his body reacted like this? The reassurance helped briefly, enough for him to settle for a little while, but uncertainty returned quickly. He did not experience these questions as excessive. From his perspective, he was trying to verify something important. If other people could tell him he was fine, then maybe he could believe it for a moment.

When the tension built beyond what he could manage, Mateo sometimes hurt himself physically to release the intensity. He described these moments not as a wish to die, but as desperate attempts to interrupt feelings that had become too large and too activated in his body. The physical pain gave him a short-lived sense of relief and containment, something concrete he could focus on when everything inside him felt keyed up and unmanageable. Even then, he often checked himself afterward, monitoring his body closely and asking others whether he seemed alright.

Over months, these patterns began to reshape his life. At work he became known as intense and easily startled, and he started dreading situations where people moved unpredictably around him. He had trouble staying present in collaborative settings because some part of his attention was always assigned to scanning the environment and his own body. In his relationships, friends grew used to the repeated need for reassurance, though Mateo could tell some of them did not understand why he could not simply accept their answers and move on. That gap left him feeling more alone.

What finally brought him to treatment was the accumulation of strain: the constant tension in his body, the way he reacted to sudden movement in ordinary settings, and the fear that he could not stop monitoring himself or needing others to steady him. He came in wanting relief, but also wanting to understand why his body still lived as if the war zone were near. What frightened him most was the sense that he might never be able to let his guard down, that even in a conference room or among friends he would remain poised for danger. At the same time, he was hoping for something simple and profound: to move through a day without feeling that every shift around him, and every sensation inside him, had to be treated like a warning.
